Line 1a: 'Notiora' stands awkwardly and may belong with the preceding clause, and the sentence beginning 'Qua de re quoniam' does not complete its construction until 'unde'; 'acquiritur' is read as printed, though the edition suggests 'aperitur' ('is opened'). Line 2a: the words 'You have rejected...' are cited by the edition as Matt. V, 9, but the saying corresponds to Mark 7:9 (compare Matt. 15:3). 'quas' is read as 'quibus' as the edition suggests. Line 3a: 'incest' renders 'incestum', here unchastity violating consecration. 'si tamen poenitens poenitenda faciat' is obscure in sense. Line 4: the construction shifts between singular and plural, and 'ad velamen solemnitatis ordinem' is awkward and may be corrupt. 'misericordia' may mean almsgiving. Line 5: 'adulterum sexum' is odd, since 2 Timothy refers to women; the text may have read 'alterum' ('the other sex'). The subject of 'repetunt' is unclear. 'Id de sacerdotibus' may be a marginal heading or a corruption. The edition's 'Supple sic' is followed at 'populum [thus]'. The closing question is incomplete in sense and may be corrupt. Throughout, 'sacerdos' can cover bishops as well as presbyters. Line 6: 'disci ne' is read as 'disciplinam'. 'subjacere contendere' is rough, and the Latin may be damaged; the reference is to sexual activity.

Editorial matter in the printed text, namely the editor's proposed variants and cross-references to Nicaea and Siricius, has been left out; proposed readings are followed where they are evident. Ref. 8: the citation of II Cor. VI, 9 is as printed; the words are from I Cor. VI, 9. Ref. 9: 'estbgenitrici suet' is read as 'est genitrici suae'; the passage is Cant. VI, 8, not I, 8 as printed. 'De tradentium persona' is taken as those conferring baptism. Ref. 10: 'illius' is taken as the bishop. Ref. 11: 'dicrum' is read as 'dierum'. The passage is obscure, especially 'multus in hoc proficit sermo', and the sense is tentative. Ref. 12: the Old Testament law cited concerns a dead brother's wife, though the heading concerns a wife's sister. The questions about Jacob and 'those who had wives and concubines' are elliptical. The citation Matt. XVII, 11 is as printed; the saying is at Matt. XIX, 11. Ref. 13: the last sentence seems damaged, and 'it' is supplied for what the people bestow. Ref. 14: the text is obscure and may be corrupt. 'Filiam' (daughter) sits oddly after the heading's 'uxorem' (wife), and the clause 'similis causa generando per gradus patris extranei separatur atque purgatur' is rendered tentatively. Ref. 4a: 'Quisque' is taken as 'whoever'. Ref. 17: 'legero' is read as 'legem'.

Section 18: the syntax of 'ordinationes celebrare praeceptis metropolitanum episcopum non permittere' is awkward and the text may be corrupt; a footnote mark 'c' stands before 'praeceptis', and '[to act]' is supplied. 'Sedis apostolicae' sits oddly after 'episcopalem moderationem' and is translated as it stands. The 318 bishops are those of the Council of Nicaea. Read 'amplius' for 'amplias', 'pudoris'-type scanning breaks were joined, and 'Praeterea' for 'Praterea'. Section 20: 'ut certa sunt' is taken as 'as they are fixed'; a footnote mark precedes 'observentur', and the wording may be doubtful. The phrase 'vere Deus in nobis est' echoes I Cor. XIV, 25. The final passage (ref. 5a) is not part of the canons: it is a later editor's remark on Siricius, placed here in the library's text. In it 'parentem' is rendered 'father' as a term of respect.

nodes.text: LETTER X.
OR, CANONS OF THE SYNOD OF THE ROMANS TO THE BISHOPS OF GAUL.

I. On a virgin who has already been veiled in Christ, and likewise on one who has not yet been veiled. II. That priests should become a pattern of good works for their peoples; on the chastity and continence of priests; and on one who has served as a soldier in the world. III. On the custom of the Roman Church regarding the clergy; and that catholic bishops ought to have one confession and one discipline. IV. On the sacrament of baptism and exorcised oil, and on one who has married his wife's sister. V. On those who have obtained worldly power. On one who has married his uncle's wife. On the ordination of clerics. And on clerics of other [churches]. VI. Likewise on a bishop who oversteps his own boundaries. On excommunicated laymen who have been made clerics by another bishop.

1. That knowledge of the truth must be sought; that it is reached through prayers. Among the other saving commands by which the Lord exhorts and admonishes his disciples, the apostles, to the hope of life, as the words of the Gospel have also taught us, he commands this too: that we should labour earnestly to reach the knowledge of the truth. And first, that we should come to know what is unknown, not by empty progress but by labour and earnest care, and that what is not yet known must be investigated through prayers. He taught that the better known things, but also those that are difficult, must be sought insistently; that what is closed, one ought to ask in prayer to have unlocked for oneself, knocking by the power of faith. For so it is written: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you (Matt. VII, 7). Certainly no one who does not ask receives, and no one who does not seek finds; and to one who has not knocked, it cannot be opened. On this matter, then, since what is asked for in faith is granted; and what was obscure is gained as clear to the understanding while it is investigated; and what was closed to us is revealed by knocking more often, that is, by entreating. For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened (ibid.): hence to repeat the same things is no trouble to me, and for you it is necessary.

2. That by changing traditions one falls into heresy. Traditions are rendered in reply to the questions put forward. We know, dearest brothers, that many bishops in various churches, to the very bad repute of their own name, have hastened through human presumption to change the tradition of the fathers, and for this reason have fallen into the darkness of heresy, since they delight in seeking the glory of men rather than in having God's rewards. Now therefore, since it is not for the sake of testing but for the sake of strengthening the faith that your holiness has deigned to inquire, on the authority of the apostolic see, about the knowledge of the law and the traditions, wishing us to make plain more freely the explanation of the questions put forward, which you seek sincerely and with longing: listen. So far as the divine favour shall fill me, I shall set out, though in modest speech yet with firm sense, what is to be held, in order indeed to correct all the divergences in which arrogance alone has presumed to create discord, as divine Scripture says: You have rejected the commandment of God, in order to establish your traditions (Matt. V, 9). If therefore you desire with sound faith to recognise the true observances, deign to attend willingly to what I say. In the first place, the matter of modesty and chastity is put before me. After that, the many questions gathered together will be set out. And so to the individual propositions, each in its order, the traditions must be rendered in reply.
CHAPTER I. 3. On a veiled virgin who has changed her commitment, what has been judged. It is asked concerning veiled virgins who have changed their commitment what has been judged about this.

If a virgin already veiled to Christ, who has professed her integrity by public testimony and has received the veil of blessing from a priest with prayer poured forth, either commits incest secretly, or, wishing to shield her crime, has given an adulterer the name of husband, taking the members of Christ and making them members of a prostitute (I Cor. V, 15), so that she who had been the bride of Christ should be called the wife of a man: in a woman of this kind there are as many charges of guilt as there are grounds: the commitment to integrity changed, the veil lost, the first faith corrupted and brought to nothing. What kind of satisfaction, and how great, is needed here! How great a penance for her who has incurred the destruction of the flesh! It is no small fault to have abandoned God and gone after a man. For this reason she must weep for very many years, so that, when worthy fruit of penance has been produced, she may at some time be able to come to pardon, provided that as a penitent she does what is to be repented of.

4. What of a girl not yet veiled who has likewise fallen from her commitment. Likewise a girl who has not yet been veiled, but had resolved to remain so: although she has not been veiled in Christ, yet because she made the resolution, and was not veiled in marriage, it is called a clandestine marriage, because she did not keep the precept of the heavenly marriage, as love hurried on to the blindness of lust. And for these a period for doing penance must be set: since, whether carried off or willing, she consented to go to a man in a perverse order, and, no testimony of relatives or priests having been gathered, such persons did not keep with chaste modesty the solemn order for the veil; rather, they acted against the precept of the Old Testament. Those whom the law commanded to be stoned (Deut. XXII, 24) are now, since that punishment has ceased, struck spiritually: so that, being as if dead, they may not enter the Church. Yet they have room for doing penance, though they do not quickly have pardon; for if the girl had cried out according to the law, and, protesting at length, had held herself back, she would certainly have been free from fault. It is therefore fitting that both be suspended from communion under the same fixed period, and do worthy penance, redeeming the crime committed by weeping, humility, fasting and mercy.

CHAPTER II. 5. That bishops, priests and deacons are bound by the law of continence. And indeed our discourse has already often flowed through many churches concerning such matters, above all concerning priests, whose merit requires that they be a pattern of their good works for their peoples. But as far as I understand, since Scripture says, Speak into the ears of those who hear, we will pour into their ears by instructing them. While they often repeat the same things that are held in neglect by each person, this is truly what was said to the adulterous sex: Always learning, and never reaching the knowledge of the truth (II Tim. III, 7). For when what is usefully advised is not kept, the apostolic commands are despised as if unknown; yet the judgment on what they have committed cannot be changed. This concerning priests. In the first place it has been decreed concerning bishops, presbyters and deacons, who must be present at the divine sacrifices, by whose hands both the grace of baptism is handed on and the body of Christ is confected; whom not only we but also divine Scripture compels to be most chaste, and whom the fathers too ordered to be bound to keep bodily continence; and on this matter let us not pass over but state the reason also. For with what shame has a bishop or presbyter dared to preach integrity or continence to a widow or virgin, or to urge her to keep a chaste bed, if he himself has pressed on to beget sons for the world rather than for God? Adam, who did not keep the commandment, was cast out of paradise and lost the kingdom (Gen. III, 23); and do you think that a transgressor can reach the heavenly kingdoms? For this reason Paul says: You are no longer in the flesh, but in the spirit (Rom. VIII, 9); and again: And let those who have wives be as though they did not have them (I Cor. VII, 29). Or would he who exhorts the people [thus], flattering Levites and priests, grant them licence to perform the work of the flesh, the same man who says: And make no provision for the flesh in its desires (Rom. XIII, 14); and elsewhere: But I would wish all to be as I myself am (I Cor. VII, 7)? He who serves as a soldier of Christ, who sits in the seat of the teacher, who cannot keep the discipline of his service?

6. That worshippers of idols, when about to sacrifice to demons, imposed continence on themselves. Concerning these three grades, therefore, which we read of in the Scriptures, it has been commanded that purity be observed by the ministers of God, for whom the need is always at hand. For either baptism must be administered or sacrifices must be offered (See Siricius, letter 1, ch. 7, and Innocent, letter 6, no. 2). Will an unclean man dare to defile what is holy, when the things that are holy are holy for the holy? Indeed, those who offered sacrifices in the temple, so as to be clean, remained in the temple for a whole year, solely for the merit of observance, wholly unacquainted with their own homes. Certainly idolaters, in order to carry out their impieties and sacrifice to demons, impose on themselves continence from women, and wish to purify themselves from foods as well: and you ask me whether a priest of the true God, who is to offer spiritual sacrifices, ought to be perpetually purified, or whether, wholly in the flesh, he ought to take care for the flesh? If intercourse is pollution, then certainly the priest, who is to make petition for the sins of others, must stand prepared for the heavenly office, lest he himself be found unworthy. For if it is said to laypeople: Abstain for a time, so that you may be free for prayer (I Cor. VII, 5), and they at any rate serve creation by begetting, priests can have such a name, but they cannot have the merit. But if this is so, and the presumption persists, then the discipline of bishops or presbyters or deacons must now be associated with the life of publicans. Wherefore, my dearest ones, I warn, as reverence for religion itself urges, that the mystery of God ought not to be entrusted to men of this kind, defiled and faithless, in whom the holiness of the body appears polluted through filth and incontinence. For just reason also sets these apart. Let them certainly hear: That flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God, nor corruption incorruption (I Cor. XV, 50). And does a presbyter or deacon dare to strive to submit in the manner of animals?

7. That one who, as one of the faithful, serves as a soldier for the world is not free from injustice. Likewise concerning him who, already one of the faithful, has served in worldly military service: it is known that he makes use of public liberty. For who can keep watch over him? Who can deny either that he has been present at the spectacles, or that, driven by the advantage of money, he could not have been free from violence and injustice?

CHAPTER III.—8. That one who has fallen into fornication after baptism must not be admitted to the clergy. The Roman Church specially observes this: that if anyone baptized as a little child has preserved the integrity of the body, he may be admitted to the clergy; or if anyone has been baptized as an adult and has remained chaste, the husband of one wife, he may become a cleric, if he is bound by no other chains of crimes. But as for him who has corrupted the sacraments of the water by carnal vices, even if he takes a wife after his fornication, how will he be able to assist in the ministry for forgiving sins, when he has gone back to the blindness of his former life? How is this to be understood: Neither fornicators, nor idolaters, and others of the kind, will possess the kingdom of God (II Cor. VI, 9), if there is no difference between good and evil, between just and impious, between the dissolute and the chaste, between one who observes the law and a publican? Such men will become ministers or priests not of Christ, but rather of Antichrist. And where is that which the holy apostle Paul, who gave the pattern of a bishop, of what sort he should be when ordained, commanded beforehand, saying: Blameless, sober and chaste, etc. (I Tim. III, 2)? How is this man blameless, who could not keep the sacrament of baptism? O new presumption! The priesthood is entrusted to this man, to whom penance alone is due, so that by long satisfaction he may be able to wash clean the defiled benefits of pardon.

9. That there should be one faith and one tradition. Apostolic discipline has established that there ought to be one confession of catholic bishops. If then there is one faith, there ought also to remain one tradition. If there is one tradition, one discipline ought to be kept through all the churches. Churches have indeed been founded in different regions, but through the whole world she is called one by the unity of the catholic faith. For thus also we read: One is my dove, one is my perfect one, she is the only one of her mother (Cant. I, 8). I am writing back now, then, not about the principle of baptism, but about the person of those who confer it.

CHAPTER IV.—10. That outside Easter presbyters may confer baptism. The same licence has not been granted to deacons. At Easter time the presbyter and the deacon have been accustomed to give the remission of sins through the parishes, and to fulfil the ministry, even when the bishop is present; they also go down into the font themselves; they are in the office, but the sum of the deed is credited to his name. At other times, however, when the necessity of illness compels each person to obtain it, the presbyter specially has licence to give forgiveness of sins through the grace of the saving water, since he is also permitted to offer the gift for the sake of cleansing; but to deacons no licence is found to have been granted: yet if it happened that they once usurped this, they are said to be excused by necessity, and they are not to do it afterwards with assurance.

11. Whether the anointing with exorcized oil ought to be repeated. As for the exorcized oil, whether a brief number of days should be set: much discussion on this is of benefit. For a person is cleansed by his own full faith. For if the chrism poured on the head imparts its grace to the whole body, nonetheless also, if one examined at the third scrutiny has been touched with the oil, not often but once, God works by his power in due time.

12. That it is not permitted to take the sister of one's wife as wife. Concerning him who has taken the sister of his wife as wife: in the law of the Old Testament it is written that, to raise up seed for a dead brother, one ought to take [his] wife, but only if he had left no children by her (Deut. XXV, 5). For that is why John the Baptist spoke against Herod, because it was not lawful for him to take the wife, since she had left children by the brother (Matt. XIV, 4). Yet for the sake of male descent the ordinance of the Law commanded this to be done by a man: concerning women it is nowhere read, but perhaps presumed. For the Law says: Cursed be he who sleeps with the sister of his wife (Lev. XVIII, 18). Jacob, who had two wives at one time, sisters, for the sake of a mystery, and concubines, and all who were born were called patriarchs: is a Christian not now permitted to have this? Those who had wives and concubines? But now the Testament does not allow this to be done, where integrity is treated more fully and chastity is praised by the teaching of Christ, when he says: Not all receive the word of God, but those to whom it is given (Matt. XVII, 11).

CHAPTER V.—13. That those who have administered the law of the world are not to be admitted to the ministry of the altar. The stain of simony and popular favour are to be guarded against in elections. It is clear, moreover, that those who have obtained worldly power and administered the law of the world cannot be free from sin. For while the sword is drawn, or an unjust judgement is given, or tortures are applied as cases require, or they devote care to preparing pleasures, or attend those prepared, joining themselves anew to the things they renounced, they have altered the discipline of observance that was handed down. They do themselves much good if they do not aspire to the episcopate; but let them, doing penance for all these things, when a fixed time has been completed, earn association with the altars. At the Council of Nicaea, with the divine Spirit assenting, when the confession of faith had been rightly established, the bishops gathered together wished the apostolic traditions also to come to the knowledge of all, defining among other things (can. 1) that a castrated man should not become a cleric, since the castrated man and the effeminate shall not enter the sanctuary of God (Deut. XXIII, 1). Then they commanded that, after the grace of baptism, after the forgiveness of sins, when anyone has gloried in the military service of the world, or one who has delighted in the purple and the fasces, he should by no means be admitted to the priesthood by any irruption. For it is by merits and observances of the law that men reach the summit of such dignity; no one will be able to arrive there by the money of Simon, or by influence, or by popular favour. For what is sought is not what the people want, but what the discipline of the Gospel wants. The people have valid testimony whenever, rejecting the breeze of favour, they bestow it on the merit of someone worthy.

14. That it is not permitted to take the wife of one's maternal uncle as wife. Likewise concerning him who has taken the wife of his maternal uncle as wife. It is not permitted to take the daughter of a maternal uncle as wife: since a similar case is separated and purged in begetting through the degrees of the father of an outsider, but it is unlawful to go back again. For one who has presumed to violate the bed of his father or mother: this is not called marriage, but fornication.

But whoever has usurped the right to act against the apostolic canons must be deprived of the priesthood, if he is obstinate; but if he has corrected himself, let what was presumed be done away with, so that, reconciled, he may have fellowship with us.

15. That laymen should not be advanced to the episcopate. Concerning ordinations it must be especially observed that bishops should always be made from clerics. For thus it is written: And let these first be tested, and so let them minister (I Tim. III, 10). He who is not proved to have ministered in a lesser office in the time before, how is he set over the clergy? It has not been heard of, nor has it yet happened, that a recruit has taken up the command of soldiers. So that man ought to be made [bishop] whom age, time, merit and life commend. Or why does the Apostle forbid a neophyte (ibid. 6), and not permit hands to be laid quickly on anyone (I Tim. V, 22)?

16. That no one should move from church to church. Likewise, those who pass from church to church were ordered to be regarded as if they had left their wife and gone to another man's; which cannot go unpunished. They ordered that such a bishop, an invader of another's chastity, be deprived of the episcopate.

CHAPTER VI.—17. That clerics rejected by their own bishop are not to be received or promoted by others.—Likewise concerning clerics of others, it has frequently been discussed and confirmed by synod, and just reason constrains us, that clerics cast out of the church by their own bishop cannot receive even lay communion in another church, as has been confirmed and made clear, since even an innocent man, without letters from his bishop or a *formata* [letter of commendation], cannot minister in another church. But if anyone presumes to do this to the injury of a priest, and is willing to receive or promote a condemned cleric, let him know that he has shared in the sins of others and has incurred the sentence of the Apostle, who says that not only those who act against the law are guilty, but also those who consent with those who act (Rom. I, 32). Therefore it must be left to the conscience of him who has judged concerning his own cleric, knowing that God will judge concerning his judgement hereafter. Hear the Lord saying: For what you wish men to do to you, do the same to them also (Matt. VII, 12). Why do you arm yourself to the injury of your brother and fellow priest? For when a guilty cleric who has been cast out is not only received but also promoted, the bishop is judged unjust. Whoever does this, let him know that he is shut out from the fellowship of Catholics and can no longer have the communion of the apostolic see.

18. That it is not permitted to celebrate ordinations in another's territory. Moreover this too is quite serious, and against the episcopal moderation of the apostolic see: to go beyond one's own boundaries, to make for another's region, to hurry, to celebrate ordinations, [and] by orders not to permit the metropolitan bishop in his own diocese, together with the neighbouring bishops, [to act], as the 318 bishops confirmed that three or more priests ought to ordain a bishop or appoint the worthiest man in his place. Certainly if anyone has invaded the boundaries of another's property, he is judged guilty of violence. Why this running? Why this hurrying, that the church's rule should be trampled underfoot? Human laws are held to, and divine precepts are despised. The present sword and temporal punishment are feared, but divine vengeance, which holds the everlasting flames of Gehenna, is neglected. You will have to see for yourselves what presumption has done. From now on, if anyone dares to presume to perform an ordination in another's diocese, let him know that he who has presumed to invade another's church can be endangered in his own standing. This is not something of the world; these are not worldly promotions. Let us hear the Apostle saying: Lay hands quickly on no one, and do not share in the sins of others: keep yourself chaste (I Tim. V, 22). If the writings were read, and the fear of God were in us, all scandals could be removed, and unanimity could stand firm among all the brothers, peaceful and full of charity.

19. That laymen excommunicated by their own bishop should not be advanced to the clergy by another. Moreover, it is also said that laymen who have been shut out of communion after their case was heard have been made clerics by another bishop: this is now beyond every evil. Therefore let those who have dared to do such things either, on being called to account, correct [it], so that those on whom the order was unworthily conferred are removed, or let their names be reported to us, so that we may know from whom we ought to keep ourselves apart (Council of Nicaea, c. 5).

20. So let your sincerity know that if all these things are observed in their order, as they are fixed, God is not offended, schisms do not arise, and heresies do not appear; but the Gentiles will say that truly God is in us, Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father, with the Holy Spirit, for ages of ages everlasting. Amen.

Moreover there are two personal letters of Ambrose, bishop of Milan, namely 85 and 86, addressed to Siricius, from which it could be proved how great a friendship existed between that prelate and our pope, if it were established that the man to whom he writes is Siricius of Rome and not some other of the same name. Yet since it is by no means unclear that this man was a bishop, from the fact that Ambrose in the former letter calls him father, it may not improbably be believed that he is the one who presided over the Roman church.
